title: Superscalar Execution
summary: How a CPU fetches, decodes, and issues multiple instructions per cycle, and why going wider hits diminishing returns fast.

slides.markdown:
A **superscalar** processor fetches, decodes, and issues **multiple instructions per cycle**, not one. Where a scalar 5-stage pipeline ([classic-5-stage-pipeline](classic-5-stage-pipeline)) completes at most one instruction per cycle in the ideal case, a superscalar core duplicates the front-end and functional units so several independent instructions can move through in lockstep, cycle after cycle.

Every mainstream CPU since the 1990s (x86, ARM, RISC-V high-end cores) is superscalar — it's the baseline technique that makes modern single-thread performance possible, not an exotic add-on.

**Issue width** is how many instructions the machine can dispatch in one cycle — a 4-wide core issues up to 4 instructions per cycle. Doubling issue width sounds like doubling performance, but it rarely delivers even close to that in practice.

Why: real code doesn't offer 4 independent, ready instructions every single cycle ([ilp-fundamentals](ilp-fundamentals)). Dependence chains, branches, and cache misses leave issue slots empty far more often than a marketing spec sheet suggests — which is exactly why cores plateaued around 4–8-wide instead of climbing toward 16 or 32.

Going superscalar means duplicating pipeline hardware, not just running the clock faster.

![A superscalar pipeline with duplicated fetch, decode, and execute paths issuing two instructions per cycle](assets/superscalar-pipeline.svg)

Fetch pulls multiple instruction words per cycle, decode has parallel decoders, and execute has multiple functional units — independent instructions execute side by side, not merely fetched together and serialized.

assets.alt: A superscalar pipeline with duplicated fetch, decode, and execute paths issuing two instructions per cycle

slides.markdown:
Wider issue hits hard structural walls before dependences even become the bottleneck:

- **Duplicated functional units** — more ALUs/FPUs/load-store units cost area and power.
- **Register-file ports** — N instructions per cycle needs roughly 2N read + N write ports; ports scale area and delay badly.
- **Issue logic** — deciding *which* N of many candidates to issue, respecting all dependences, gets combinatorially harder as width grows.

These costs grow faster than linearly with width — the real reason issue width tops out well below what raw silicon budgets might allow.

| | Scalar pipeline | Superscalar pipeline |
|---|---|---|
| Max issue/cycle | 1 | N (typically 4–8 today) |
| Front-end hardware | Single fetch/decode | Duplicated N-wide |
| Bottleneck | Pipeline depth, hazards | Register-file ports, issue logic, available ILP |
| Theoretical CPI | 1 | 1/N (rarely reached) |

**How to decide:** scalar suffices where area/power dominate (embedded cores); superscalar earns its cost only where the workload has enough exploitable independent instructions to keep extra issue slots busy — which most general-purpose code does, at least partially.

slides.sectionTitle: Issue width isn't the whole story
slides.markdown:
It's tempting to treat issue width as a direct performance multiplier — "an 8-wide core is 2x an 4-wide one." It isn't. Achieved **IPC (instructions per cycle)** depends on how often the machine actually finds N independent, ready instructions to fill every slot.

A workload dominated by long dependence chains, frequent branches, or cache misses can leave a wide core's extra slots empty most cycles — its real IPC ends up far below its issue width, and a narrower core with better branch prediction or a bigger reorder buffer can outperform it on that workload.

slides.sectionTitle: Tracing dual-issue through a real block
slides.markdown:
Take four instructions on a 2-wide superscalar core (2 ALUs, 1 load/store unit):

```
I1: R1 = R2 + R3     ; ALU
I2: R4 = load [R5]   ; load/store unit
I3: R6 = R1 + R7     ; ALU, RAW on I1
I4: R8 = R4 + R9     ; ALU, RAW on I2
```

**Cycle 1**: I1 and I2 use different functional units and have no dependence on each other, so both issue together. **Cycle 2**: I3 needs I1's result — if I1 has 1-cycle latency, I3 can issue now; I4 needs I2's load result, which typically takes longer (2-4+ cycles for an L1 hit), so I4 must wait. Only I3 issues this cycle — the pair collapses to single-issue because the *other* ready instruction (I4) isn't actually ready.

This is the concrete shape of the "limited by what's ready, not just width" idea: a 2-wide machine only sustains 2 IPC when two independent, ready instructions exist **every** cycle — real code rarely provides that consistently, which is why measured IPC on wide machines runs well below issue width.

slides.sectionTitle: Numbers: where the extra ports and units go
slides.markdown:
Going wider isn't just "add more ALUs" — every doubling of issue width roughly **quadruples** the register file's port count needed (each of N instructions may need 2 reads + 1 write, so N issue slots need ~2N read ports and N write ports, and port count drives register-file area and access latency super-linearly). This is a big reason register files, not ALUs, are often the limiting structure in a wide design.

The instruction fetch and decode stages also have to keep pace: decoding N instructions per cycle means N parallel decoders, and on variable-length ISAs (x86) even finding where each instruction *starts* in a fetched block is a serial dependency that resists parallelization — one reason x86 cores cache pre-decoded micro-op traces (a decoded-µop cache/trace cache) rather than re-decoding every fetch.

In practice, real cores plateau around **4-8 wide** issue for exactly these reasons: beyond that, the area and power cost of register-file ports, decode logic, and dependence-checking hardware (which scales roughly with the *square* of window size, since every instruction potentially checks against every other) outpaces the IPC gained.

slides.sectionTitle: Structural hazards on shared functional units
slides.markdown:
Superscalar issue width is often advertised as "N-wide" as if all N slots are interchangeable, but real designs give each slot access to only a subset of functional units — a common split is 2 ALU-capable slots, 1 load/store slot, and 1 branch slot, not 4 fully general slots.

This creates **structural hazards** that have nothing to do with data dependence: four completely independent ALU instructions ready in the same cycle still can't all issue on a 2-ALU-port design — two must wait a cycle for a free unit, even though nothing about their data forces that wait. Code that happens to cluster many instructions of the same kind (a burst of loads, or a run of floating-point ops on a core with few FP ports) can starve on unit availability while the core's other ports sit idle.

This is why real-world IPC on a "6-wide" core rarely resembles 6 issued instructions per cycle on average — the achievable rate depends on the *mix* of instruction types matching the mix of available ports, not just on raw independence.
